name: pgrust (pgrcolumnar)
workload: ClickBench combined score (standard analytical query suite) run using pgrust's built-in columnar table layout, pgrcolumnar, on c8g.4xlarge (AWS Graviton4).
claimed_speedup: 18.5% faster than ClickHouse on the ClickBench combined score; 'hundreds of times faster' than stock PostgreSQL 18.3 on the same queries
compiler_and_flags: rustc, benchmark builds compiled with -Ctarget-cpu=neoverse-v2 tuned for Graviton4; published/downloadable binaries are generic and will not reproduce the exact numbers
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 copyleft license limits reuse in proprietary products; project is a from-scratch Rust reimplementation of Postgres so feature/extension parity is incomplete; the tuned Graviton4 build flag is not what ships in generic binaries
caveats: Benchmark harness lives in benchmarks/ in the repo and was reviewed independently by Greg Smith (author of 'PostgreSQL 9.0 High Performance'), but that is expert review, not an independently re-run third-party suite. Authors previously claimed >50% OLTP speedup and revised it down to 30% after finding the number varies (50-60%) on Kubernetes vs bare EC2, which they disclose as unresolved. The headline blog title '300x faster analytics' refers to a narrower micro-benchmark, not the 18.5% ClickBench combined-score figure used here.
found_via: Hacker News: search 'pgrust' / 'faster than ClickHouse' -> Show HN: Pgrust v0.2: Now faster than Postgres and Clickhouse (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49111925)

verification.tier_reason: Public harness at benchmarks/ (run-clickbench.sh, scorers/score-clickbench.py, run-oltp-ro.sh, build-pgo.sh) on branch archive/v0.2-main-2026-09-15, with rustc 1.96.0 pinned, -Ctarget-cpu=neoverse-v2 + dist profile (fat LTO) + PGO, and c8g.4xlarge Graviton4 all stated. It scores against a vendored ClickBench ClickHouse c8g.4xlarge row and runs PostgreSQL 18.3 head-to-head for OLTP. That meets A for what the kit documents, but not for the README's 18.5% figure.
verification.notes: The OLTP-vs-PostgreSQL comparison is a genuine head-to-head run by the harness. The ClickHouse win depends on pgrust's own pairwise score against a stale leaderboard row and on a README number the kit does not reproduce. Kept at A for the kit-documented figures, with claimed_speedup corrected. The orchestrator may prefer PostgreSQL as the primary baseline.
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence for the recorded claim (pgrcolumnar beats ClickHouse): the ClickBench maintainer removed all pgrust rows on 2026-09-22 (ClickBench PR #2165) for per-query kernels, plan matchers named after ClickBench queries and hot runs replaying cached filter verdicts; v0.3 ships hand-lowered plans for all 43 queries (7 answered from metadata) and refuses other query shapes. Same basis as SlothDB. Its separate OLTP result vs PostgreSQL (1.25-1.40x) is a genuine head-to-head and is noted as a lead for a later wave.

name: SlothDB
workload: Author-run comparison of SlothDB against a user-supplied DuckDB binary using bench/clickbench (the 43 ClickBench queries verbatim) and a custom bench/run.py harness, plus an earlier HN claim citing a 14GB/100M-row hits.parquet ClickBench-style comparison against DuckDB and ClickHouse.
claimed_speedup: Originally announced as 1.35x-5x faster than DuckDB and ClickHouse (HN, 2026-05-01); the project's own current README explicitly walks this back, calling README/bench numbers 'anecdotal, not from standardised benchmark hardware' and noting wins are 'query-shape-specific' due to a per-query handler-dispatch path rather than the general engine
hardware: Not stated (author says 'one workstation', no CPU model given)
tradeoffs: Early-stage/experimental per the author; no vendor PR to the real ClickBench is open; the project itself says some benchmark wins come from special-cased per-query handlers rather than the general query engine, which is a materially weaker and more overfit claim than a general engine speedup.
caveats: Self-disclosed low-confidence result: the maintainer explicitly warns readers not to treat the numbers as final and flags that they are not from standardized hardware and may reflect query-specific handler dispatch rather than a real architectural win over DuckDB/ClickHouse. Included per the 'tag instead of exclude' rule, but confidence is set low.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia query 'faster than DuckDB' -> 'SlothDB a 5X Faster Alternative to DuckDB, ClickHouse DB' (2026-05-01)

verification.tier_reason: First-party, author-run comparison against DuckDB v1.4.3 with public code (bench/clickbench/official_bench.py plus the 43 verbatim ClickBench queries). No CPU model, compiler or flags are given, and the README itself calls the numbers anecdotal, so it is C.
verification.notes: The README no longer contains any benchmark numbers. The real data is bench/clickbench/official_results.md (last changed 2026-05-19), and it shows only a modest geomean 1.24x win with correctness diffs and an aggregate loss, so I rewrote claimed_speedup. I confirmed the HN 1.35x-5x claim via HN Algolia (item 47971921). Metadata checks out: MIT, 413 stars, last commit 2026-06-03, active.
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence: the ClickBench results come from benchmark-specific fast paths, and the ClickBench maintainer disqualified the submission (ClickBench#930); the dispatch code remains in tree. Even on those results it is slower overall than DuckDB (71.1 s vs 65.2 s), Q18's 14.81x is a LIMIT without ORDER BY that returns a different answer, and sqllogictest parity is ~11-18%.

name: AnuDB
workload: Raspberry Pi: JSON-document insert/query/update/delete and parallel-operations benchmark (10,000/1,000/5,000/2,500 ops respectively) via the AnuDBBenchmark repo, AnuDB (RocksDB-backed) vs SQLite3.
claimed_speedup: ~2.34x higher ops/sec than SQLite3 in the parallel-operations test (AnuDB processed 4x more operations, 10 threads vs SQLite3's 4); AnuDB is also ~1.23x faster on queries, but SQLite3 is 3.9x faster on inserts, 2.1x faster on updates, and 5.3x faster on deletes in the same table
tradeoffs: AnuDB is a JSON-document layer built on top of RocksDB (not a from-scratch storage engine); embedded-only, no client/server mode besides an optional MQTT interface.
caveats: The project's Show HN title claimed "279x Faster Than SQLite in Parallel Workloads," but that figure does not appear on the linked benchmark page/repo, whose own table shows only a ~2.34x parallel advantage with unequal thread/op counts between engines, and SQLite winning most other categories outright. Reported here using only the number that is actually on the page, per the hard rule against inventing numbers.
found_via: HN Algolia: query="embedded key-value store" tags=story -> "Show HN: AnuDB– Backed on RocksDB, 279x Faster Than SQLite in Parallel Workloads", cross-checked against https://github.com/hash-anu/AnuDBBenchmark

verification.tier_reason: The numbers are first-party, from the AnuDBBenchmark README (anusqlite_benchmark.cpp) on an unnamed Raspberry Pi. The build script gives no -O level, and the SQLite and RocksDB static-lib flags are unstated, so at most C. On substance, SQLite wins insert, update and delete by 2.1-5.3x, and neither 'win' holds up. In the parallel test AnuDB took 1.71x longer wall time (1429 s vs 835 s), and SQLite's op count is cut because 3 of its 4 threads failed to commit (no busy_timeout, contended transactions). The 1.23x query 'win' has AnuDB returning only doc IDs while SQLite reads the json_data column of every row.
verification.notes: Rejected as not-faster on invalidity grounds, as with fastestjsoninthewest: the numbers are on the page, but the two 'wins' come from a broken SQLite harness (failed commits; AnuDB slower by wall time) and asymmetric query work, and SQLite wins the rest. If the orchestrator keeps it under the flagged-entries policy, use tier C with the corrected claimed_speedup and caveats. Metadata checks out: MIT, 56 stars, last commit 2025-06-24 (stale).
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence: the parallel 2.34x is an artifact (both sides used 4 threads, not 10 vs 4; 3 of 4 SQLite threads failed to commit, and AnuDB's wall time was 1429 s vs SQLite's 835 s). The 1.23x query result compares returning IDs only against returning json_data; SQLite wins inserts, updates and deletes; the HN 279x claim is unsupported.

name: StrikeMQ
workload: Internal micro-benchmarks (benchmarks/ dir, strikemq_bench binary) of a single-node, Kafka-wire-compatible broker: 1KB log append, SPSC ring push+pop, and Kafka protocol header decode.
claimed_speedup: Log append 1KB: 83ns p50 / 4.4us p99.9; SPSC ring push+pop 42ns p99.9; Kafka header decode 42ns p99.9; broker startup <10ms and 0% idle CPU, contrasted with Kafka's JVM/ZooKeeper cold start; no direct side-by-side number against a running Kafka instance is given on the page
tradeoffs: Explicitly positioned as a dev/test stand-in ('like LocalStack for AWS'), not for production load; single-node only, no replication or consumer-group durability guarantees comparable to real Kafka; only latency/micro-op numbers are published, no throughput numbers.
caveats: Numbers are self-reported micro-benchmarks of internal components (log append, ring buffer, header decode) rather than a measured comparison against a running Kafka broker on shared hardware; small hobby project (14 stars), no stated compiler/CPU for the benchmark run.

verification.tier_reason: The README Performance table lists absolute timings for internal components only: 83 ns p50 / 4.4 us p99.9 log append, 42 ns ring push+pop, 42 ns header decode, and <10 ms startup. benchmarks/latency_bench.cpp only times StrikeMQ's own ring buffer, log and codec. No Kafka number is measured or quoted anywhere (README, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, PRODUCT.md, CHANGELOG.md or the Show HN post), so there is no comparative evidence against the baseline.
verification.notes: The record's numbers and metadata are accurate: MIT, 14 stars, last commit 2026-02-12, not a fork, not archived, and CMake Release uses -O3 -march=native -flto. The Kafka contrast is only qualitative ('JVM, ZooKeeper/KRaft, gigabytes of RAM, slow startup'). The project is a dev/test stand-in, not a claimed faster broker, and it is also not notable (14 stars; the Show HN post got 3 points).
